title: Worksheet 1: Uncovering Confounding with Simpson’s Paradox
text: Hello class. This worksheet is designed to give you hands-on practice with the concepts we discussed in Lecture 1. The goal is not just to get the right answer, but to understand the process of thinking causally.

title: Worksheet 1: Uncovering Confounding with Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Background / Scenario
A hospital has conducted a study comparing two treatments for kidney stones:

Treatment A: A new, advanced surgical procedure.
Treatment B: The standard, less invasive treatment.

The hospital has provided you with data on 400 patients who received one of the two treatments. The outcome of interest is whether the treatment was a success (i.e., the kidney stones were completely removed).

title: Worksheet 1: Uncovering Confounding with Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Learning Objective
By the end of this worksheet, you will be able to:

Calculate and compare crude (overall) rates of success.
Identify a potential confounding variable from a problem description.
Perform a stratified analysis to calculate group-specific rates.
Explain how confounding can lead to Simpson’s Paradox, where group-specific trends are reversed in the aggregate data.
Draw a simple Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) to represent the relationships between variables.

title: Worksheet 1: Uncovering Confounding with Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Step-by-Step Scaffolding Tasks

Step 1: The Naive (Overall) Comparison
First, let’s look at the data from a purely associational perspective, ignoring any other factors.

Task 1a: Calculate the overall success rate for patients who received Treatment A.

Guiding Question: What is the total number of patients who had a success with Treatment A? What is the total number of patients who received Treatment A?
Calculation: (Number of Successes for A) / (Total Number receiving A) = ?

Task 1b: Calculate the overall success rate for patients who received Treatment B.

Calculation: (Number of Successes for B) / (Total Number receiving B) = ?

Task 1c: Based only on these overall rates, which treatment appears to be more effective?




Step 2: Identifying a Potential Confounder
In our lecture, we discussed that observational comparisons can be misleading. A key piece of information was left out of the table above: doctors tend to assign the more invasive Treatment A to patients with large kidney stones, while patients with small stones often receive the standard Treatment B. Stone size is also known to affect the difficulty of the treatment.

Task 2a: In this scenario, what is the third variable that might be related to both the treatment assigned and the treatment’s success? This is our potential confounder.
Task 2b: Explain why this variable could be a confounder.

Guiding Question: How might stone size influence a doctor’s choice of treatment? How might stone size independently influence whether a treatment is successful?





Step 3: The Stratified Analysis (Controlling for the Confounder)
Now, let’s re-examine the data, but this time we will “stratify” it by stone size. This is like looking at the data for small stones and large stones separately.
Here is the complete data, broken down by stone size:

Task 3b: Calculate the success rate for each treatment only for patients with large stones.

Success Rate for A (Large Stones): ? / ? = ?

Step 4: Visualizing the Causal Structure (DAG)
Let’s draw a map of our causal assumptions.

Task 4: Create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) with three nodes: Treatment Choice, Stone Size, and Success. Draw arrows to represent the causal relationships you uncovered in the steps above.

Guiding Questions:

Does the treatment choice cause a successful outcome? (This is the arrow we hope to understand). Draw it.
Does the patient’s stone size cause the doctor to choose a particular treatment? Draw it.
Does the stone size cause a treatment to be more or less successful, regardless of which treatment is used? Draw it.

title: Worksheet 1: Uncovering Confounding with Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Reflection / Discussion Questions

Compare your answer from Task 1c with your answers from Task 3a and Task 3b. What do you notice? This reversal is known as Simpson’s Paradox.
Explain, in your own words, why Treatment A looked worse in the overall analysis but better in both the small-stone and large-stone groups. (Hint: Think about which group of patients was disproportionately receiving Treatment A).
What does this exercise teach you about the danger of drawing causal conclusions from simple, overall comparisons of two groups in observational data?

title: Worksheet 1: Uncovering Confounding with Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Optional Challenge
Imagine a different variable: Post-operative Care Unit. Suppose all patients who get Treatment A are sent to ICU Care, while patients getting Treatment B are sent to Standard Care. A researcher decides to “control” for this by stratifying the analysis by care unit. Why might this be a mistake? Think about the timing. Can the choice of care unit be a common cause of both treatment and success, or is it something else? (This touches on the concept of a mediator, which we will discuss later in the course).

title: How to Write a Great Critique
text:
Welcome to the central guide for your weekly paper critiques. The goal of this assignment is to train you not just to understand a paper, but to deconstruct its argument, question its assumptions, and situate it within the broader field of causal inference.
Our course uses a unique mix of readings: foundational methodological papers, applied case studies, and modern textbook chapters. Your critique assignment asks you to focus on the foundational paper for each week, but the key to an excellent critique is to skillfully synthesize insights from all three sources.


Depending on the paper, you will need to wear one of two hats: the theoretician’s hat for methodological papers or the peer reviewer’s hat for case studies.


(Applies to papers like Rubin 1974, Pearl 1995, Rosenbaum & Rubin 1983)
When a paper proposes a method, your critique should focus on the validity, logic, and impact of that method. Since there is no data analysis, you must analyze the abstract argument.
Use this four-step process to structure your thinking:

Deconstruct the Problem & Proposed Solution:

The Problem: What specific challenge in causal inference is the paper trying to solve? (e.g., How can we control for many confounders at once? How do we define a causal effect?)
The Solution: What is the paper’s core contribution? Explain the new concept (e.g., potential outcomes, propensity scores, DAGs) in your own words.

Analyze the Logic & Identification Strategy:

The “Why”: What is the central logical argument for why their solution works? Explain the intuition behind any theorems or proofs. (e.g., The authors prove the propensity score is a balancing score, meaning…)
The Assumptions: What are the precise assumptions needed for this logic to hold? (e.g., This entire framework rests on the untestable assumption of strong ignorability…)

Scrutinize the Assumptions & Plausibility:

Real-World Plausibility: In what kinds of real-world studies would these assumptions be plausible? Where would they likely fail? Use examples from the case study or your own knowledge.
Failure Modes: What are the practical limitations of the method? (e.g., The method offers no protection against unmeasured confounding and is sensitive to violations of the positivity assumption.)

Evaluate the Impact & Legacy:

The Impact: How did this paper change the field? What did it make possible?
The Legacy: What subsequent research or methods did it inspire? What is its biggest remaining limitation?





(Applies to papers like Yusuf et al. 1991, Snowden et al. 2011, and all of the “Expedition” readings)
When a paper makes a causal claim about the world using data, your critique should focus on the credibility of that claim. Your job is to act as a rigorous, skeptical peer reviewer.

Scrutinize the Causal Question & Design:

The Question: Is the causal question well-defined (PICO)? Is the target trial clear?
The Data: Is the data source appropriate? Are there risks of major measurement error?

Interrogate the Identification Strategy:

The DAG: Draw a DAG for this specific study, reflecting its variables and context.
Attack the Key Assumption: This is the core of your critique. Is the central assumption (e.g., unconfoundedness, parallel trends, exclusion restriction) plausible in this specific context? What unmeasured confounder or alternative explanation did the authors likely miss?

Audit the Diagnostics & Analysis:

The Diagnostics: Did the authors perform and show the essential diagnostic checks for their method? (e.g., balance plots for propensity scores; first-stage F-statistic for IV).
The Model: Was the statistical model appropriate for the outcome and data structure?

Challenge the Interpretation & Conclusion:

The Interpretation: Do the authors overstate their claims? Do they acknowledge their key limitations?
The Sensitivity Analysis: Did they quantify how robust their finding is to unmeasured confounding (e.g., with an E-value)? If not, it is a major weakness.
The Generalizability: Do they correctly interpret the scope of their finding (e.g., acknowledging a LATE is not an ATE)?






Your assignment is to critique the foundational paper. You will use the other readings to become a smarter critic.
Your Task: Critique Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983), “The central role of the propensity score…”

Start with the Map (Textbook): You read Hernán & Robins, Chapter 12. You now have a modern understanding of propensity scores, the ATE, and balancing diagnostics.
Critique the Journal (Foundational Paper): You apply the “How to Critique a Foundational Paper” framework to Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983).

Problem: The paper addresses the problem of controlling for many confounders in observational studies.
Solution: It introduces the propensity score as a single-number summary for balancing covariates.
Logic: It proves the balancing property of the score.
Assumption: The entire method relies on the assumption of strong ignorability (unconfoundedness).

Enrich with the Expedition (Case Study): Now, you use Dehejia & Wahba (1999) to add depth to your critique.

In your section on Assumption Plausibility, you write: “Rosenbaum & Rubin’s framework is entirely dependent on the unconfoundedness assumption. The Dehejia & Wahba (1999) case study provides an ideal scenario where this assumption is arguably plausible. By using a rich administrative dataset with detailed pre-treatment earnings and employment histories, they were able to control for the most likely determinants of both entering the training program and future earnings.”
In your section on Impact & Legacy, you write: “A key limitation of the original paper is its focus on theory, with little guidance on diagnostics. The profound impact of this work is demonstrated in applications like Dehejia & Wahba, which established the now-standard practice of reporting standardized mean differences in a balance plot to empirically verify that the propensity score did, in fact, balance the observed covariates.”


By following this process, you are not critiquing the case study; you are using it as evidence to make your critique of the foundational paper more concrete, critical, and insightful.

section: STAT 579: Rubric for Weekly Paper Critiques
text:
STAT 579: Rubric for Weekly Paper Critiques
This rubric outlines the criteria for evaluating your weekly paper critiques posted on the Canvas Discussion forum. The goal is to reward thoughtful engagement with the material, clear reasoning, and a critical, assumption-focused perspective.

1. Rubric for Student Critiques (Participants)
This rubric is for all students who are not the designated Discussion Leader for the week. Each critique is worth a total of 20 points.










Dimension
Excellent (A-Level Work)
Good (B-Level Work)
Needs Improvement (C-Level or Below)
Points




Answers to Guiding Questions
Answers are not just correct but demonstrate deep, critical engagement with the paper. The student uses examples, connects concepts to the broader course, and writes with analytical depth.
Answers are generally correct and address all parts of the prompt. The analysis is sound but may be more descriptive than critical.
Answers are incomplete, factually incorrect, or demonstrate a superficial understanding of the core concepts.
/ 12


Clarity & Reasoning
The writing is clear, logical, and easy to follow. The student effectively communicates complex statistical ideas in their own words.
The writing is mostly clear, but may contain some jargon or slightly convoluted phrasing. The core logic is sound.
The writing is unclear, making the argument difficult to follow. Key terms may be used incorrectly.
/ 4


Takeaway & Critical Perspective
The takeaway is insightful, goes beyond a simple summary, and shows critical reflection on the paper’s assumptions, limitations, or broader implications.
The takeaway is reasonable and relevant to the paper, but may not offer a deep or novel insight.
The takeaway is a simple restatement of a fact from the paper, is unrelated to the core argument, or is missing.
/ 4





2. Rubric for the Weekly Discussion Leader
The weekly Discussion Leader is evaluated on the same 20-point scale but with criteria re-weighted to reflect their role in framing the conversation for the class.










Dimension
Excellent (A-Level Work)
Good (B-Level Work)
Needs Improvement (C-Level or Below)
Points




Summary & Synthesis
The summary is comprehensive, accurate, and skillfully frames the paper’s context, core argument, and importance. It provides a strong foundation for the class discussion.
The summary is accurate and covers the main points but may lack depth in explaining the paper’s broader significance or context.
The summary contains significant inaccuracies, is incomplete, or fails to identify the paper’s central contribution.
/ 8


Answers to Guiding Questions
Answers are exemplary, serving as a model of deep analysis for the class. They are well-reasoned and demonstrate a superior grasp of the material.
Answers are correct and thoughtful, addressing all parts of the prompt.
Answers are superficial, incorrect, or suggest a misunderstanding of the guiding questions.
/ 6


Posing New Questions
The two self-generated questions are insightful, open-ended, and designed to stimulate high-level discussion and critical thinking beyond the provided questions.
The questions are relevant but may be more straightforward or less provocative (e.g., closer to comprehension checks).
The questions are simple comprehension checks, are unclear, unrelated to the core themes, or are missing.
/ 6

title: STAT 579: Project Proposal Grading Rubric
text:
This rubric outlines the criteria for evaluating your project proposal. The proposal is graded out of 50 points and accounts for 10% of your final course grade. The goal of this deliverable is to ensure that you have a well-defined, feasible, and causally-grounded research plan.










Component
Weight
Criteria for Excellence (A)
Criteria for Proficiency (B)
Criteria for Developing (C/Below)




Causal Question & Motivation
10 pts
The causal question is specific, clear, and unambiguous. The motivation is compelling, grounded in public health/scientific relevance, and supported by appropriate citations.
The question is causal but could be more specific. The motivation is present but may be overly broad or not well-supported.
The question is associational, vague, or poorly defined. The motivation is unclear or absent.


Data Source
10 pts
The proposed dataset is clearly identified and is appropriate for the causal question. Key variables (exposure, outcome, confounders) are correctly identified.
A dataset is identified, but its appropriateness is not fully justified. The list of key variables may be incomplete.
No specific dataset is identified, or the chosen dataset is clearly unsuitable for the research question.


Causal Model (DAG)
15 pts
The DAG is plausible, clearly drawn, and includes the key exposure, outcome, and confounders. The justification for the DAG’s structure is thoughtful and demonstrates a strong understanding of the topic.
The DAG is present but may be overly simplistic or contain questionable causal arrows. The justification is superficial.
The DAG is missing, illegible, or fundamentally incorrect (e.g., contains cycles, reverses obvious causal pathways).


Target Trial Protocol
10 pts
The key components of the target trial (eligibility, treatment strategies, outcome) are clearly and precisely defined, demonstrating a strong grasp of the emulation framework.
The target trial components are listed but may be vague or poorly aligned with the causal question and data.
The target trial protocol is not described or is fundamentally misunderstood.


Proposed Method(s) & Feasibility
5 pts
The proposed causal method is appropriate for the question and data. The plan is feasible within the scope of the course, and potential challenges are acknowledged.
A causal method is proposed but may not be the most appropriate. The feasibility of the plan is questionable.
No causal method is proposed, or the proposed method is incorrect for the stated problem.

title: STAT 579: Final Project Proposal
text:
This document serves as the proposal for the STAT 579 final project. The goal is to provide a clear, concise, and feasible plan for your target trial emulation. Please replace the instructional text (in italics) with your own content. The final proposal should be approximately 2-3 pages.

1. The Causal Question

State your primary research question in a single, clear sentence. It must be a causal question (e.g., “What is the causal effect of X on Y?”) and not merely associational.



2. Scientific Background and Motivation

In 1-2 paragraphs, explain the public health or scientific relevance of your question. Why is this an important question to answer? What is already known on the topic? Briefly cite 2-3 key references that motivate your study.



3. Data Source

Identify the observational dataset you will use. Describe the source of the data (e.g., NHANES 2017-2018 cycle, MIMIC-IV v2.0). List the key variables you plan to use for your exposure (A), outcome (Y), and the primary confounders (L) you identified in your DAG.



4. Preliminary Causal Model (DAG)

Insert an image of your Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) here. The DAG should represent your current understanding of the causal relationships between the exposure, outcome, and key covariates. Below the image, provide a brief (1 paragraph) justification for the structure, explaining the most important causal pathways and confounding variables.



5. Target Trial Emulation Protocol

Briefly outline the key components of your target trial protocol. You can do this in a bulleted list. This does not need to be exhaustive at this stage, but it should be specific.

Eligibility Criteria: e.g., “Adults aged 40-75 with no prior history of CVD.”
Treatment Strategies: e.g., “Initiate a statin within 30 days of the index date” vs. “Do not initiate a statin.”
Outcome: e.g., “Incidence of myocardial infarction or stroke within 5 years of follow-up.”




6. Proposed Causal Method(s)

In one paragraph, state the primary causal method you intend to use to estimate the effect (e.g., propensity score weighting, g-computation). Briefly explain why this method is appropriate for your question and data structure. Mention any key diagnostics you plan to perform (e.g., covariate balance checks).

title: How To Find a Dataset for Target Trial Emulation
text:
Welcome to the data exploration hub for your final project. Finding the right dataset is arguably the most important step in a successful causal inference study. A good dataset doesn’t just have interesting variables; it must have the right structure to allow for the emulation of a target trial.
This page provides you with two things: a powerful tool for searching broadly and a curated list of datasets that are known to be well-suited for this kind of work.

title: How To Find a Dataset for Target Trial Emulation
section: The Go-To Tool: Google Dataset Search
text:
The Go-To Tool: Google Dataset Search
Think of this as Google Scholar, but for data. The Google Dataset Search engine indexes thousands of data repositories from around the world. It is the best place to start when you have a specific topic in mind.
Launch Google Dataset Search 

Tips for Effective Searching
When searching, use keywords that describe the structure of the data you need, not just the topic. Good causal inference requires data where time is well-defined.

Combine your topic (e.g., “cancer”, “education”, “air pollution”) with structural keywords like:
“longitudinal study”
“cohort study”
“prospective data”
“panel data”
“linked mortality data”

title: How To Find a Dataset for Target Trial Emulation
section: Curated Datasets for Target Trial Emulation
text:
Curated Datasets for Target Trial Emulation
Not all datasets are created equal. The best datasets for TTE are longitudinal cohort studies, where a group of people is enrolled at a baseline point in time and followed forward. This structure allows us to properly define eligibility, measure confounders before treatment, and follow individuals for the outcome.
Here are a few high-quality, publicly-available datasets that are exceptionally well-suited for your project.

Framingham Heart Study

Why it’s great for TTE: This is the archetypal prospective cohort study. A cohort of residents from Framingham, MA, was enrolled in 1948 and has been followed ever since. It contains detailed baseline measurements of potential confounders (e.g., smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure) and tracks cardiovascular outcomes over many decades. It’s a perfect dataset for emulating a trial of an intervention (e.g., lifestyle change, medication) on heart disease.
Access: Data is available to researchers through a proposal process. Visit the Framingham Heart Study Website.



MIMIC-IV (Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care)

Why it’s great for TTE: This database of ICU admissions contains high-resolution, time-stamped data. This is critical because you can precisely define time zero (e.g., time of admission, time of a specific diagnosis). Treatments (medications, ventilators) and outcomes are all logged with precise timing, allowing you to emulate a trial of a clinical intervention in a critical care setting and avoid biases like immortal time bias.
Access: Requires completion of a human subjects research training course. Visit the MIMIC-IV Website.



Add Health (The National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health)

Why it’s great for TTE: This is a classic longitudinal cohort. A representative sample of U.S. adolescents was enrolled in 1994-95 and has been followed into adulthood. This is ideal for questions where the “treatment” occurs in adolescence (e.g., participation in sports, a specific educational program) and the outcome occurs in adulthood (e.g., income, health status). The baseline wave contains rich data on potential confounders (family background, school environment, etc.).
Access: Public-use data is readily available. Visit the Add Health Website.



NHANES (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey) with Linked Mortality Data

Why it’s great for TTE: By itself, NHANES is a series of cross-sectional surveys. However, participants can be linked to the National Death Index. This transforms the dataset into a prospective cohort study. You can use the rich survey data at baseline (diet, lab values, lifestyle) to define eligibility and measure confounders. You can then emulate a trial where the outcome is long-term mortality.
Access: Data is publicly available from the CDC. Visit the NHANES Website.

title: How To Find a Dataset for Target Trial Emulation
text:
✅ Checklist for Evaluating a Dataset
When you find a dataset that looks promising, use this checklist to assess its suitability for a Target Trial Emulation project.

Can you define a clear time zero? Is there a variable that marks the start of follow-up for all individuals (e.g., date of enrollment, date of diagnosis, start of the school year)?
Are confounders measured at or before time zero? The fundamental requirement for confounding control is that your covariates are measured before the treatment is assigned.
Is the exposure/treatment variable well-defined? Can you clearly determine who is “treated” and “untreated” based on the data?
Is the outcome measured after time zero? The dataset must have follow-up data to ascertain the outcome after the intervention.
Is the follow-up period long enough? Is there sufficient time between treatment and outcome for a causal effect to plausibly occur?

If you can answer “yes” to these questions, you likely have a strong candidate dataset for your project.

title: Introduction to Causal Inference
text:
Welcome to Week 8. Our journey in causal inference has so far centered on a fundamental question: What is the total effect of an exposure (\(A\)) on an outcome (\(Y\))? We have invested heavily in methods—propensity scores, standardization, IPW—to answer “if” and “how much” a treatment works. Now, we pivot to a question that is often of greater scientific importance: How does it work?
Mediation analysis is the statistical methodology for investigating causal mechanisms. It allows us to open up the “black box” between an exposure and an outcome to understand the pathways, or intermediate steps, through which a causal effect is transmitted. We decompose a total effect into its constituent parts, isolating the portion that acts through a specific intermediate variable (the mediator) from the portion that acts through all other channels.
Consider a public health campaign (\(A\)) designed to increase weekly physical activity (\(Y\)). The program’s designers hypothesize that the campaign works primarily by increasing participants’ self-efficacy (\(M\)) to overcome barriers to exercise. Mediation analysis provides the tools to formally test this hypothesis. We can ask:

What is the total effect of the campaign on physical activity?
How much of that effect is transmitted through changes in self-efficacy? This is the indirect effect, representing the specific mechanism we want to quantify.
How much of that effect is due to other pathways? (e.g., the campaign also builds social support networks, or simply reminds people to exercise). This is the direct effect.

Understanding mechanisms is not merely an academic exercise; it is crucial for building better science and more effective policy.

Scientific Theory: Mediation analysis allows us to test hypotheses derived from scientific theory. If a drug is thought to work by targeting a specific biological receptor, we can test if the biomarker for that receptor’s activity mediates the drug’s effect on the disease.
Intervention Optimization: If we find that 90% of the campaign’s effect is mediated through self-efficacy, future versions could be streamlined to focus on this core component, potentially saving costs and increasing impact. Conversely, if the direct effect is large, it suggests other powerful mechanisms are at play that we should identify and leverage.
Identifying Harmful Pathways: An intervention could have a beneficial total effect, but one of its pathways could be harmful. For example, a weight-loss drug might have a beneficial direct effect on metabolism but also a harmful indirect effect by increasing blood pressure. Mediation analysis can uncover these competing effects.

This chapter will equip you with the conceptual and practical tools to conduct mediation analysis. However, a word of caution: this power comes at a cost. As we will see, identifying mediated effects requires strong, untestable assumptions, particularly about unmeasured confounding between the mediator and the outcome. Therefore, a critical and humble approach is essential.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Define and distinguish between direct, indirect, and total effects using the potential outcomes framework.
Represent and interpret mediation pathways using Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs).
Differentiate between “controlled” and “natural” effects and understand their respective policy implications.
Estimate mediated effects using both traditional (product-of-coefficients) and modern (causal mediation) approaches in R.
Clearly state and critically evaluate the key assumptions for identifying mediation effects, particularly the four assumptions of sequential ignorability.
Conduct and interpret a sensitivity analysis to assess the robustness of your findings to violations of key assumptions.

title: Introduction to Causal Inference
text:
2. Key Concepts and Causal Pathways

The Mediation Triangle
The foundational structure of a mediation analysis is the “mediation triangle,” a simple DAG that illustrates the hypothesized causal relationships between the exposure (A), the mediator (M), and the outcome (Y).
      A (Exposure)
      /   \
     /     \
    v       v
   M (Mediator) -> Y (Outcome)

Exposure (\(A\)): The treatment, intervention, or exposure of interest.
Mediator (\(M\)): An intermediate variable on a causal path from A to Y. For a variable to be a mediator, it must be causally influenced by A and, in turn, causally influence Y. The temporal ordering is critical: A must precede M, and M must precede \(Y\).
Outcome (\(Y\)): The final outcome of interest.

The DAG encodes specific causal hypotheses:

The Direct Pathway (\(A\rightarrow Y\)): This arrow represents the causal effect of the exposure on the outcome that does not pass through the mediator M. It is the sum of all other causal mechanisms.
The Indirect Pathway (\(A\rightarrow M\rightarrow Y\)): This two-arrow path represents the causal effect of the exposure on the outcome that is transmitted through the specified mediator M.



Total, Direct, and Indirect Effects: A Potential Outcomes Perspective
To define these effects rigorously, we turn to the potential outcomes framework.

Total Causal Effect (TE): This is the familiar effect of changing the exposure from a reference level (0) to an active level (1) on the outcome.

\[
\text{TE} = E[Y(1) - Y(0)]
\]
Where Y(a) is the potential outcome for Y that would be observed if an individual were assigned exposure level a.

Decomposing the Total Effect: To decompose the TE, we must introduce a more complex type of potential outcome that depends on both the exposure and the mediator: \(Y(a,m)\). This represents the potential outcome that would be realized if the exposure were set to level \(a\) and, simultaneously, the mediator were set to level m. We also define \(M(a)\) as the potential value of the mediator if the exposure were set to level \(a\).


Controlled vs. Natural Effects
This distinction is fundamental to modern mediation analysis and clarifies the precise causal question being asked.

Controlled Direct Effect (CDE): The CDE quantifies the effect of the exposure while the mediator is experimentally controlled or fixed to a specific level, m, for all individuals in the population.

\[
\text{CDE}(m) = E[Y(1, m) - Y(0, m)]
\]
Causal Question: “What would be the effect of the treatment if we could intervene to hold everyone’s mediator value constant at level m?” For example, in a study of a statin drug (A) on heart attacks (Y) mediated by LDL cholesterol (M), the CDE(100) would be the drug’s effect if everyone’s cholesterol could be forced to 100 mg/dL. This is policy-relevant for setting clinical targets but may not be biologically or practically feasible.

Natural Direct and Indirect Effects (NDE & NIE): These effects are often of greater scientific interest because they are defined by the “natural” levels of the mediator that would occur under treatment or control, rather than a single fixed value.
Natural Indirect Effect (NIE): This is the core quantity for assessing mediation. It captures the portion of the treatment’s effect that works by changing the mediator.

\[
\text{NIE} = E[Y(1, M(1)) - Y(1, M(0))]
\]
Causal Question: “What change in the outcome would be observed if we held an individual’s exposure status constant at ‘treated’ (\(A=1\)) but could change their mediator from the level it would naturally take under control (\(M(0)\)) to the level it would naturally take under treatment (\(M(1)\))?” This isolates the effect transmitted only through the \(A \rightarrow M\) pathway.

Natural Direct Effect (NDE): This captures the portion of the treatment’s effect that does not operate through the mediator \(M\).

\[
\text{NDE} = E[Y(1, M(0)) - Y(0, M(0))]
\]
Causal Question: “What would be the effect of the treatment if we could somehow block the pathway through \(M\) by holding the mediator for everyone at the level it would have naturally taken in the absence of treatment (\(M(0)\))?”
Under the assumption of no interaction between the exposure and the mediator on the outcome, the total effect decomposes perfectly:
\[
TE=NIE+NDE
\]
When an interaction exists, a third term representing the joint effect of both pathways is also present. The modern causal mediation framework handles this decomposition gracefully.

title: Introduction to Causal Inference
text:
3. Methods and Estimation Approaches

The Traditional Approach: Product and Difference Methods
The classical approach to mediation, popularized by Baron and Kenny (1986) and rooted in path analysis, provides an intuitive method for linear models without exposure-mediator interaction.
Consider the following system of linear equations:

Mediator Model: \(E[M∣A]=\alpha_0+\alpha_{1}A\)
Outcome Model: \(E[Y∣A,M]=\beta_0+\beta_{1}A+\beta_{2}M\)
Total Effect Model:\(E[Y∣A]=\tau_{0}+\tau_{A}\)

The effects are estimated as follows:

Indirect Effect:
Product of Coefficients: The indirect effect is the product of the path coefficients from \(A\) to \(M\) (\(\alpha_1\)) and from \(M\) to \(Y\) (\(\beta_2\)).

\[
\text{Indirect Effect} = \alpha_1 \times \beta_2
\]

Difference in Coefficients: The indirect effect is the difference between the total effect (\(\tau\)) and the direct effect (\(\beta_1\)).

\[
\text{Indirect Effect} = \tau - \beta_1
\]
In a linear system without omitted variables, these two methods are mathematically equivalent. By substituting the mediator model into the outcome model, we see that \(\tau=\beta_1+(\alpha_1\times\beta_2)\), which proves their equivalence.

Direct Effect: The coefficient for \(A\) in the outcome model that controls for \(M\).

\[
\text{Direct Effect} = \beta_1 
\]






Example: The Difference Method



Suppose we are studying a weight loss intervention (A). We want to see if its effect on weight loss (Y) is mediated by an increase in weekly exercise hours (M).

We first regress \(Y\) on \(A\):
lm(Y ~ A) yields a coefficient for \(A\) of \(\hat\tau=−5.0\). This is the total effect: the program is associated with a 5 kg weight loss.
We then regress Y on both A and M:
lm(Y ~ A + M) yields a coefficient for A of \(\hat\beta_1=−2.0\). This is the direct effect.
The indirect effect is the difference: \(\text{IE}=\tau−\beta_1=−5.0−(−2.0)=−3.0\).

Interpretation: Of the total 5 kg weight loss, 3 kg is estimated to be due to the pathway through increased exercise, and 2 kg is due to other pathways.








Warning



Limitations of the Traditional Approach
This method is simple but fragile. Its validity hinges on strong assumptions:

Linearity: All relationships must be correctly specified as linear.
No Interaction: The effect of the mediator on the outcome (\(\beta_2\)) cannot depend on the level of the exposure A. If it does, the decomposition fails.
Model Compatibility: The method struggles with incompatible model types, such as a continuous mediator and a binary outcome (logistic regression).





The Modern Approach: Causal Mediation Analysis
The framework by Imai, Keele, and Tingley (2010) overcomes these limitations. It is a simulation-based approach grounded in the potential outcomes definitions of NDE and NIE.
The estimation algorithm proceeds as follows:

Fit a model for the mediator given the exposure and pre-treatment covariates: \(P(M∣A,X)\).
Fit a model for the outcome given the exposure, mediator, and pre-treatment covariates: \(P(Y∣A,M,X)\). These models can be of any standard type (lm, glm, etc.).
Simulate Potential Outcomes: The algorithm uses the fitted models to simulate potential outcomes for each individual under different counterfactual scenarios. For example, to calculate \(E[Y(1,M(0))]\):

For each individual \(i\), predict their mediator value under control: \(\hat M_i(0)\) using the mediator model with \(A=0\).
Predict their outcome using the outcome model with \(A=1\) but with the mediator value set to \(\hat M_i(0)\).

Average and Decompose: Average these simulated potential outcomes across all individuals to compute the Average Causal Mediated Effect (ACME, which is the NIE) and Average Direct Effect (ADE, which is the NDE).
Uncertainty Estimation: Repeat steps 3-4 many times via non-parametric bootstrapping to generate empirical confidence intervals for the ACME, ADE, and Total Effect.

This approach is powerful because it is flexible, directly estimates the quantities of interest (NDE and NIE), and correctly handles interactions and various data types.

title: Introduction to Causal Inference
text:
4. Assumptions and Identification
For our estimates to have a causal interpretation, we must satisfy four key assumptions, collectively known as Sequential Ignorability. These are strong and untestable.
Let’s consider a DAG that includes a set of pre-exposure covariates, \(X\).
      X (Covariates)
     /|\
    / | \
   v  v  v
  A -> M -> Y
  ^--------'






Assumption 1: No Unmeasured Confounding of the Exposure-Outcome Relationship



\[
Y(a,m)⊥A∣X
\]
Explanation: Conditional on the pre-exposure covariates X, the assignment to exposure level A is independent of the potential outcomes. This is the standard “no unmeasured confounding” assumption for total effects. We need to have measured and adjusted for all common causes (X) of the exposure and the outcome.








Assumption 2: No Unmeasured Confounding of the Exposure-Mediator Relationship



\[
M(a)⊥A∣X
\]
Explanation: Conditional on the pre-exposure covariates \(X\), the assignment to exposure level \(A\) is independent of the potential value of the mediator. We need to have measured and adjusted for all common causes (\(X\)) of the exposure and the mediator. Assumptions 1 and 2 are often combined.








Assumption 3: No Unmeasured Confounding of the Mediator-Outcome Relationship



\[
Y(a,m)⊥M∣A,X
\]
Explanation: This is the most critical and fragile assumption. It states that, conditional on the observed exposure (\(A\)) and pre-treatment covariates (\(X\)), there are no unmeasured factors that are common causes of the mediator (\(M\)) and the outcome (\(Y\)).
Example of a Violation: In our job training study, imagine an unmeasured trait like “intrinsic motivation” (U). A highly motivated person might respond better to the training, leading to higher interview confidence (M). That same motivation might also lead them to network more effectively, independently boosting their earnings (Y). This creates a spurious association between M and Y that would be incorrectly attributed to mediation.
  A -> M -> Y
       ^   ^
       |   |
       +---U---+








Assumption 4: No Mediator-Outcome Confounder is Itself Affected by the Exposure



Explanation: There must be no common cause of the mediator and outcome that is, itself, on the causal pathway from the exposure. Suppose the job training program (A) not only boosts confidence (M) but also causes participants to develop a new social network (L). If this new network (L) both helps them prepare for interviews (affecting M) and provides job leads (affecting Y), then L is a post-treatment confounder of the \(M-Y\) relationship. We cannot adjust for L, because doing so would block a portion of the very causal effect we want to estimate.






Warning



Consequences of Violating Assumptions 3 & 4
Violating assumption 3 or 4 will lead to biased estimates of the direct and indirect effects. Because these assumptions involve unmeasured variables or complex post-treatment dynamics, they can never be definitively proven. This is why sensitivity analysis is not optional; it is a required component of any credible mediation analysis.

title: Introduction to Causal Inference
text:
5. Numerical and Code-Based Example (R)
Let’s implement a full causal mediation analysis using the mediation package. We’ll use a simulated dataset where a job training program (A) is hypothesized to increase annual earnings (Y) by improving an individual’s confidence in job interviews (M). We also control for a pre-treatment measure of education (X).

Step 1: Simulate the Data
# Load Necessary Library
# install.packages("mediation")
library(mediation)

# Set Seed for Reproducibility
set.seed(123)

# Number of Individuals
n <- 500

# Pre-treatment Covariate: Education (in years)
X <- rnorm(n, mean = 12, sd = 2)

# Treatment Assignment (1 = Program, 0 = control)
# Assume Treatment is More Likely for Those with less Education
A <- rbinom(n, 1, prob = plogis(1 - 0.2 * X))

# Mediator: Interview Confidence (scale 1-10)
# A Has a Positive Effect on M
# X also Has a Positive Effect on M
M <- 3 + 2.5 * A + 0.5 * X + rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)

# Outcome: Annual Earnings (in $1000s)
# A Has a Direct Effect
# M Has an Effect
# There is also an A*M Interaction
Y <- 20 + 5 * A + 4 * M - 1.5 * A * M + 1.5 * X + rnorm(n, sd = 5)

# Create a Data Frame
sim_data <- data.frame(Y, A, M, X)
head(sim_data)


Step 2: Fit the Mediator and Outcome Models
We fit the two regression models that form the basis of the analysis. Note that the outcome model out.fit correctly includes the exposure-mediator interaction term (A * M), which is crucial for flexibility.
# Model 1: Mediator Model (regress M on A and X)
med.fit <- lm(M ~ A + X, data = sim_data)
# This Model Estimates the A -> M Path

# Model 2: Outcome Model (regress Y on A, M, the Interaction, and X)
out.fit <- lm(Y ~ A * M + X, data = sim_data)
# This Model Estimates the A -> Y and M -> Y Paths

summary(med.fit)
summary(out.fit)


Step 3: Run the Mediation Analysis
We pass the two fitted models to the mediate() function. We specify the treatment (treat = "A") and mediator (mediator = "M") variables. We request bootstrapped confidence intervals, which are essential for robust inference.
# Perform Causal Mediation Analysis
# Sims = 500 is Good for a Quick Check, Use 1000+ for Final Results
med.analysis <- mediate(med.fit, out.fit, treat = "A", mediator = "M", boot = TRUE, sims = 1000)


Step 4: Interpret the Results
The summary() function provides the key decomposition of effects.
summary(med.analysis)
Example Output:
Causal Mediation Analysis

Potential Outcome Simulation based on the given models

(Details about the models)

                Estimate 95% CI Lower 95% CI Upper p-value
ACME (control)     8.63         7.48         9.83    <2e-16 *
ACME (treated)     4.88         3.83         6.02    <2e-16 *
ADE (control)      8.75         6.93        10.51    <2e-16 *
ADE (treated)      5.00         3.63         6.43    <2e-16 *
Total Effect      13.63        11.93        15.42    <2e-16 *
Prop. Mediated    0.63         0.54         0.74    <2e-16 *
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘*’ 0.001 ‘’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
The presence of an interaction term in out.fit means the effects differ depending on the reference group. The (control) and (treated) labels refer to which group’s potential outcomes are used as the reference. Let’s focus on the (treated) estimates, as they are often more policy-relevant (effects relative to the treated state).

ACME (Average Causal Mediated Effect / NIE): The average indirect effect is estimated to be $4.88k. This is our primary finding: we estimate that the job training program increased annual earnings by $4,880 through its effect on interview confidence. The 95% CI [3.83, 6.02] is well above zero, providing strong evidence for this mechanism.
ADE (Average Direct Effect / NDE): The average direct effect is $5.00k. This means that an additional $5,000 of the program’s earnings benefit comes from pathways other than changes in interview confidence. The 95% CI [3.63, 6.43] is also clearly positive.
Total Effect: The total effect of the program is an estimated $13.63k increase in earnings, which is the sum of the NIE and NDE (when defined carefully to account for interaction).
Prop. Mediated: Approximately 63% of the total effect is mediated by interview confidence under one definition. This provides a simple, powerful summary: confidence-building is the dominant mechanism of this program’s success.

title: Introduction to Causal Inference
text:
6. Sensitivity Analysis
We must now challenge our result by assessing its vulnerability to violations of Assumption 3 (no unmeasured M-Y confounding). Sensitivity analysis asks: “How strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be to change our conclusion?”
The medsens() function operationalizes this by examining rho, the correlation between the error terms of the mediator and outcome models. A non-zero rho represents the net effect of all unmeasured M-Y confounders.

Performing and Visualizing the Sensitivity Analysis
# Perform Sensitivity Analysis
sens.analysis <- medsens(med.analysis, rho.by = 0.05, sims = 200)

# Get a Detailed Summary
summary(sens.analysis)

# Plot the Results for a Visual Check
plot(sens.analysis, "rho")
Interpreting the Output:
The plot shows the estimated ACME (indirect effect) on the y-axis as a function of rho on the x-axis. The solid line is the point estimate, and the dashed lines are the 95% confidence interval.
The critical question is: At what value of rho does the 95% CI for the ACME cross zero?
The summary output will state this value explicitly. For our example, let’s say the summary reports: ACME is zero at rho = 0.65.
Interpretation: This is a very reassuring result. It means that an unmeasured M-Y confounder would need to be strong enough to induce a correlation of 0.65 between the residuals of our mediator and outcome models to nullify our finding of a positive indirect effect. A confounder this powerful is often considered implausible in many social science contexts. We can therefore conclude that our finding is relatively robust to potential unmeasured confounding. Conversely, if the analysis showed the effect was zero at rho=0.1, our conclusion would be deemed sensitive and far less credible.

title: Introduction to Causal Inference
text:
7. End-of-Chapter Exercises

Conceptual Questions

Draw a DAG for a study examining whether a new blood pressure medication (A) reduces the risk of heart attack (Y). Propose a plausible biological mediator (M) and at least one potential pre-treatment confounder (X) and one potential unmeasured M-Y confounder (U). Explain precisely which assumption the presence of U violates.
Explain the difference between a Controlled Direct Effect and a Natural Direct Effect in intuitive terms, using the example from question 1. Which is usually of greater scientific interest and why?
A colleague uses the Baron-Kenny method and finds no significant indirect effect. However, you suspect there is a strong interaction between the treatment and the mediator. Explain why their null finding might be misleading and what you would recommend they do instead.



Numerical Problem
A researcher conducts a study on the effects of a mindfulness app (A=1 for app, A=0 for control) on student anxiety (Y, measured on a 100-point scale), mediated by hours of sleep per night (M). They use linear models with no interaction term and report the following coefficients from their lm() outputs:

Model lm(Y ~ A): Coefficient for A is -12.0.
Model lm(M ~ A): Coefficient for A is 1.5.
Model lm(Y ~ A + M): Coefficient for A is -6.0; coefficient for M is -4.0.

Using the product-of-coefficients and difference-in-coefficients methods, calculate the Total Effect, Direct Effect, and Indirect Effect. What proportion of the total effect is mediated by sleep?


R Coding Task
Using the sim_data created in this chapter, create a binary outcome variable Y_binary <- ifelse(Y > median(Y), 1, 0). Fit a logistic regression model for the outcome (glm(…, family = “binomial”)). Run the mediate() function and interpret the ACME and ADE. How does the interpretation of effects on a probability scale differ from the interpretation on a continuous scale?

title: Introduction to Causal Inference
text:
8. Appendix: Advanced Derivations

Formal Decomposition of the Total Effect
The total effect, \(\text{TE}=E[Y(1)−Y(0)]\), can be decomposed by adding and subtracting a counterfactual quantity, \(E[Y(1,M(0))]\).
\[
TE=E[Y(1)−Y(0)]=E[Y(1)−Y(1,M(0))]+E[Y(1,M(0))−Y(0)]
\]
By the consistency assumption, we can state that an individual’s potential outcome Y(a) is that which would be observed if their exposure is a and their mediator is the value it would naturally take on under exposure a, i.e., Y(a)=Y(a,M(a)). Applying this:

The first term becomes \(E[Y(1,M(1))−Y(1,M(0))]\), which is the definition of the NIE.
The second term, \(E[Y(1,M(0))−Y(0)]\), can be rewritten as \(E[Y(1,M(0))−Y(0,M(0))]\) by applying consistency to Y(0), which is the definition of the NDE.
Thus, we arrive at the fundamental decomposition:

\[
TE=NIE+NDE
\]


Delta Method for Variance of the Indirect Effect (Sobel Test)
In the traditional product-of-coefficients approach (\(\text{IE}=\alpha_1\times\beta_2\)), the variance of the indirect effect is approximated using the multivariate delta method. Assuming the estimators \(\hat\alpha_1\) and \(\hat\beta_2\) are independent, the variance is:
\[
Var(α^{1​}β^{​2​})≈α^12​Var(β^​2​)+β^​22​Var(α^1​)
\]
The standard error is the square root of this quantity. A Z-statistic can then be formed for a hypothesis test (\(Z=\frac{\hat\alpha_1\hat\beta_2}{\text{SE}(\hat\alpha_1\hat\beta_2)}\)). This is known as the Sobel test. It is known to have poor performance in small samples and is generally superseded by bootstrapping, which does not rely on large-sample approximations.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
So far, we have focused on methods like regression adjustment, matching, and weighting. All these methods share a common, crucial assumption: ignorability. They require us to believe that we have successfully measured and controlled for all common causes of the treatment and the outcome.
But what if we can’t? What if there is a powerful, unmeasured confounder that we simply do not have in our dataset? This could be something like “patient motivation,” “physician skill,” or “innate ability.” In these cases, our previous methods will fail to produce an unbiased causal estimate.
This week, we introduce Instrumental Variables (IV), a brilliant and powerful method for estimating causal effects even in the presence of unmeasured confounding. The core idea is to find a “natural experiment” or a “random nudge” that affects the treatment but is not itself related to the outcome, except through its effect on the treatment.
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Identify situations where unmeasured confounding makes standard methods inappropriate.
Define an instrumental variable and articulate its three core assumptions.
Explain the intuition behind IV estimation using the Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) method.
Implement IV estimation in R using the ivreg package.
Understand what the IV method actually estimates: the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE).
Recognize and diagnose the problem of “weak instruments.”

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
section: 🧠 Key Concepts: Hacking Causality with a “Nudge”
text:
🧠 Key Concepts: Hacking Causality with a “Nudge”

The Enduring Problem: Unmeasured Confounding
Let’s consider a classic question: What is the causal effect of completing a college degree (D) on future earnings (Y)?
A simple regression of earnings on education will likely be biased. Why? Because individuals with higher innate ability (U) are both more likely to finish college and more likely to earn more, regardless of their education.
Since “ability” is nearly impossible to measure, it becomes an unmeasured confounder, creating a backdoor path (\(D \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y\)) that we cannot close with standard methods.


The IV Solution: Finding a Clean Pathway
The IV approach seeks to find a variable—the instrument (Z)—that “nudges” people into treatment but is itself unrelated to the confounder.
An instrumental variable is a variable Z that affects the outcome Y only through its effect on the treatment D.
A classic example is using geographic proximity to a college as an instrument for education. People who live closer to a college (Z) may be more likely to attend (D), but where they live is probably not related to their innate ability (U).


The Three Core IV Assumptions
For a variable Z to be a valid instrument, it must satisfy three conditions:

Relevance: The instrument must have a causal effect on the treatment.

\(Cov(Z, D) \neq 0\)
Intuition: Proximity to a college must actually affect the probability that someone attends college. An irrelevant instrument is useless. We can and should test this with data.

Exclusion Restriction: The instrument must affect the outcome only through the treatment. It cannot have a direct effect on the outcome.

Intuition: Living near a college cannot directly increase your earnings. It can only do so by making you more likely to get a degree. This is a strong assumption and cannot be proven with data; it must be justified by theory and domain knowledge.

Exchangeability (or Independence): The instrument must not share any common causes with the outcome. It must be “as-if” randomly assigned with respect to the unmeasured confounders.

\(Cov(Z, U) = 0\)
Intuition: The types of people who live near a college cannot be systematically different (in terms of ability) from those who live far away.








Justifying the IV Assumptions is Key



The validity of an IV analysis rests entirely on the plausibility of these three assumptions. While relevance can be tested, the exclusion restriction and exchangeability are untestable assumptions that you must defend based on institutional knowledge and logical argument.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
✅ Numerical Example: Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS)
The most common IV estimator is Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS). The intuition is beautiful: we “cleanse” the endogenous treatment variable of its correlation with the unmeasured confounder.
Imagine our goal is to estimate: \(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D + \epsilon\)
But we know \(D\) is correlated with \(\epsilon\) (because of U).
Stage 1: Isolate the “Clean” Variation in Treatment First, we predict the treatment D using only our instrument Z.
\[
D = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 Z + \nu
\]
The predicted values from this regression, \(\hat{D}\), represent the part of the treatment that is “exogenous”—i.e., the part that is purely driven by our “as-if” random instrument.
Stage 2: Estimate the Causal Effect Second, we regress the outcome Y on the predicted treatment from Stage 1.
\[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \hat{D} + \epsilon'
\]
Because \(\hat{D}\) is, by construction, uncorrelated with the unmeasured confounder U, the resulting estimate of \(\beta_1\) is our unbiased IV estimate of the causal effect.

A Worked Example in R
Let’s simulate data for the education-earnings example. We’ll set the true causal effect of education to 5 (e.g., $5,000).
# Load necessary libraries
library(dplyr)
library(ivreg)
library(AER) # Contains the dataset we'll use

# --- 1. Simulate data with an unmeasured confounder ---
set.seed(123)
n <- 1000
# Z: Instrument (Proximity to college, 1=close, 0=far)
# U: Unmeasured confounder (Ability)
# D: Treatment (Gets a degree)
# Y: Outcome (Earnings)
data <- tibble(
  Z = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
  U = rnorm(n, 0, 1),
  # Treatment depends on the instrument Z and ability U
  D = rbinom(n, 1, pnorm(0.5 * Z + 1.5 * U - 0.5)),
  # Outcome depends on treatment D and ability U. True effect of D is 5.
  Y = 10 + 5 * D + 3 * U + rnorm(n, 0, 2)
)

# --- 2. OLS (Naive) Regression ---
# This is biased by the unmeasured confounder U
ols_model <- lm(Y ~ D, data = data)
summary(ols_model)
# The coefficient on D is ~8.1, which is badly biased upwards from the true value of 5.

# --- 3. IV Regression using 2SLS ---
# The syntax for ivreg is Y ~ treatment | instrument(s)
# It performs both stages for us automatically.
iv_model <- ivreg(Y ~ D | Z, data = data)
summary(iv_model)
# The coefficient on D is now ~4.9, very close to our true effect of 5!

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
section: 📘 IV in the Potential Outcomes Framework: What is the LATE?
text:
📘 IV in the Potential Outcomes Framework: What is the LATE?
The IV estimate is not the Average Treatment Effect (ATE). Instead, it is the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE). To understand this, we need to define four types of people in our population relative to the instrument:

Compliers: These are individuals who take the treatment if encouraged by the instrument, and don’t if they are not. (They comply with the “nudge”).
Always-Takers: These individuals will take the treatment regardless of the instrument’s value.
Never-Takers: These individuals will never take the treatment, regardless of the instrument.
Defiers: These individuals do the opposite of what the instrument encourages. (This group is generally assumed not to exist).

The LATE theorem (Angrist & Imbens, 1994) states that the IV estimate is the average treatment effect only for the compliers.

Concept Check
Let’s use a military draft lottery as an instrument for veteran status to study the effect of military service on health. Who are the “compliers”?
Answer: The compliers are the men who would only serve in the military if they were drafted, but would not volunteer otherwise. The IV estimate gives us the effect of military service only for this specific subgroup, not for the always-takers (volunteers) or never-takers (those who would avoid service even if drafted).







The Problem of Weak Instruments



A “weak instrument” is an instrument that satisfies the exclusion and exchangeability assumptions, but is only weakly correlated with the treatment (the Relevance assumption is weak).

Consequence 1: The IV estimate becomes biased in the direction of the OLS estimate.
Consequence 2: The standard errors of the IV estimate become very large.

Rule of Thumb: In the first stage regression (D ~ Z), check the F-statistic for the significance of the instrument. If the F-statistic is less than 10, you likely have a weak instrument problem.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV)
section: 📚 Appendix: Advanced Statistical Derivations and Theory
text:
📚 Appendix: Advanced Statistical Derivations and Theory

📕 Derivation of the Simple IV Estimator
Motivation: This derivation shows how the ratio of two covariances can produce a consistent estimator for the causal effect \(\beta_1\) in the presence of an unmeasured confounder.
The Model: Assume the true structural model is:

\(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D + U\) (where U is the unmeasured confounder)
\(D = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 Z + V\) (where Z is the instrument)

We assume the key IV property: \(Cov(Z, U) = 0\). Our goal is to estimate \(\beta_1\).

Start with the covariance between the outcome Y and the instrument Z:

\[
Cov(Y, Z) = Cov(\beta_0 + \beta_1 D + U, Z)
\]

Using the properties of covariance, this expands to:

\[
Cov(Y, Z) = Cov(\beta_0, Z) + \beta_1 Cov(D, Z) + Cov(U, Z)
\]

Simplify the terms:

\(Cov(\beta_0, Z) = 0\) (covariance with a constant is zero).
\(Cov(U, Z) = 0\) (this is our crucial exchangeability assumption).

This leaves us with a simple expression:

\[
Cov(Y, Z) = \beta_1 Cov(D, Z)
\]

Solve for our target parameter, \(\beta_1\):

\[
\beta_1 = \frac{Cov(Y, Z)}{Cov(D, Z)}
\]
Conclusion: The true causal effect \(\beta_1\) is the ratio of the “reduced form” effect of the instrument on the outcome (the numerator) to the “first stage” effect of the instrument on the treatment (the denominator). The sample counterparts of these covariances form the simple IV estimator:
\[
\hat{\beta}_{IV} = \frac{\sum (Y_i - \bar{Y})(Z_i - \bar{Z})}{\sum (D_i - \bar{D})(Z_i - \bar{Z})}
\]

title: Instrumental Variables (IV) Estimation

Instrumental Variables (IV) estimation is a powerful technique for estimating causal effects when randomization is not possible due to confounding. This method allows us to identify the causal effect of a treatment on an outcome by using an instrument that affects treatment but is not directly related to the outcome. In this lesson, we will:

Understand the rationale behind IV estimation and its assumptions.
Derive the IV estimand using the potential outcomes framework.
Explain the relationship between observed outcomes and potential outcomes.
Explore the mathematical formulation of IV estimation.
Explain the expected value of observed outcomes given an instrument.
Understand the core assumption of consistency in causal inference.
Apply these concepts to practical examples.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV) Estimation
text:
Instrumental Variables (IV) estimation is a powerful technique for estimating causal effects when randomization is not possible due to confounding. This method allows us to identify the causal effect of a treatment on an outcome by using an instrument that affects treatment but is not directly related to the outcome. In this lesson, we will:

Understand the rationale behind IV estimation and its assumptions.
Derive the IV estimand using the potential outcomes framework.
Explain the relationship between observed outcomes and potential outcomes.
Explore the mathematical formulation of IV estimation.
Explain the expected value of observed outcomes given an instrument.
Understand the core assumption of consistency in causal inference.
Apply these concepts to practical examples.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV) Estimation
text:
1. Rationale and Potential Outcomes Framework
The potential outcomes framework helps us define causal effects precisely. For each individual \(i\), we define:

\(Y_i(1)\): The potential outcome if the individual receives the treatment (\(A=1\)).
\(Y_i(0)\): The potential outcome if the individual does not receive the treatment (\(A=0\)).
The individual-level causal effect is \(Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\). We can only ever observe one of these for any given person.

Similarly, we define potential treatment assignments based on the instrument, \(Z\):

\(A_i(1)\): The treatment the individual would take if the instrument is present (\(Z=1\)).
\(A_i(0)\): The treatment the individual would take if the instrument is absent (\(Z=0\)).

The challenge of confounding means that the groups who choose \(A=1\) and \(A=0\) are different in ways that also affect the outcome. The instrument (\(Z\)) helps us overcome this by creating an “as-if” random reason for changing treatment status.

IV Assumptions in Potential Outcomes

Relevance: \(\E{A(1)} - \E{A(0)} \neq 0\). The instrument actually affects treatment uptake on average.
Independence: \(Z \indep (Y(1), Y(0), A(1), A(0))\). The instrument is as-if randomly assigned and is therefore independent of an individual’s potential outcomes and potential treatment choices. This is the key assumption that replaces the “no unmeasured confounders” idea.
Exclusion Restriction: \(Y_i(a, z) = Y_i(a)\) for \(a \in \{0, 1\}\). An individual’s potential outcome depends only on the treatment they receive (\(a\)), not on the value of the instrument (\(z\)). The instrument works only through the treatment.
Monotonicity: \(A_i(1) \ge A_i(0)\) for all individuals. The instrument encourages (or has no effect on) treatment uptake for everyone; it never discourages it. This assumption rules out the existence of “defiers.”

title: Instrumental Variables (IV) Estimation
text:
2. Step-by-Step Derivation
The derivation elegantly shows how the IV formula isolates the average treatment effect for a specific group.

Step 1: Decomposing the Population
Under the monotonicity assumption, we can classify everyone into three groups based on their potential treatment choices. This is called principal stratification.

Compliers (c): Individuals who take the treatment if encouraged but not otherwise. (\(A_i(0)=0, A_i(1)=1\)).
Always-Takers (a): Individuals who take the treatment regardless of the instrument. (\(A_i(0)=1, A_i(1)=1\)).
Never-Takers (n): Individuals who do not take the treatment regardless of the instrument. (\(A_i(0)=0, A_i(1)=0\)).

Let \(\pi_c, \pi_a, \pi_n\) be the proportion of each group in the population.


Step 2: Analyzing the Numerator: \(\E{Y|Z=1} - \E{Y|Z=0}\)
First, let’s expand the term \(\E{Y|Z=1}\). The observed outcome \(Y\) when \(Z=1\) is determined by the treatment individuals take when \(Z=1\), which is \(A(1)\). So, \(Y = Y(A(1))\).
\[
\E{Y|Z=1} = \E{Y(A(1))|Z=1}
\]
By the independence assumption, we can drop the conditioning on \(Z=1\):
\[
\E{Y|Z=1} = \E{Y(A(1))}
\]
Using the law of total expectation, we can write this as a weighted average across our three groups:
\[
\E{Y(A(1))} = \E{Y(A(1))|\text{type}=c}\pi_c + \E{Y(A(1))|\text{type}=n}\pi_n + \E{Y(A(1))|\text{type}=a}\pi_a
\]
Now, substitute the known treatment status for each group when \(Z=1\):

For Compliers, \(A(1)=1\), so the term becomes \(\E{Y(1)|\text{type}=c}\pi_c\).
For Never-Takers, \(A(1)=0\), so the term becomes \(\E{Y(0)|\text{type}=n}\pi_n\).
For Always-Takers, \(A(1)=1\), so the term becomes \(\E{Y(1)|\text{type}=a}\pi_a\).

So, \(\E{Y|Z=1} = \E{Y(1)|c}\pi_c + \E{Y(0)|n}\pi_n + \E{Y(1)|a}\pi_a\).
Now we do the same for \(\E{Y|Z=0} = \E{Y(A(0))}\):
\[
\E{Y(A(0))} = \E{Y(A(0))|c}\pi_c + \E{Y(A(0))|n}\pi_n + \E{Y(A(0))|a}\pi_a
\]

For Compliers, \(A(0)=0\), so the term becomes \(\E{Y(0)|\text{type}=c}\pi_c\).
For Never-Takers, \(A(0)=0\), so the term becomes \(\E{Y(0)|\text{type}=n}\pi_n\).
For Always-Takers, \(A(0)=1\), so the term becomes \(\E{Y(1)|\text{type}=a}\pi_a\).

So, \(\E{Y|Z=0} = \E{Y(0)|c}\pi_c + \E{Y(0)|n}\pi_n + \E{Y(1)|a}\pi_a\).
Finally, we subtract the two expressions. Notice that the terms for always-takers and never-takers are identical in both equations, so they cancel out perfectly!
\[
\E{Y|Z=1} - \E{Y|Z=0} = (\E{Y(1)|c}\pi_c) - (\E{Y(0)|c}\pi_c)
\]
\[
\implies \E{Y|Z=1} - \E{Y|Z=0} = (\E{Y(1)|c} - \E{Y(0)|c}) \cdot \pi_c
\]
The numerator is the average treatment effect for compliers multiplied by the proportion of compliers.


Step 3: Analyzing the Denominator: \(\E{A|Z=1} - \E{A|Z=0}\)
This step is more straightforward. Using the same logic:
\[
\E{A|Z=1} - \E{A|Z=0} = \E{A(1)} - \E{A(0)}
\]
Let’s expand each term across our three groups:
\[
\E{A(1)} = \E{A(1)|c}\pi_c + \E{A(1)|n}\pi_n + \E{A(1)|a}\pi_a
\]
\[
\E{A(1)} = (1)\pi_c + (0)\pi_n + (1)\pi_a = \pi_c + \pi_a
\]
And:
\[
\E{A(0)} = \E{A(0)|c}\pi_c + \E{A(0)|n}\pi_n + \E{A(0)|a}\pi_a
\]
\[
\E{A(0)} = (0)\pi_c + (0)\pi_n + (1)\pi_a = \pi_a
\]
Subtracting the two gives:
\[
\E{A|Z=1} - \E{A|Z=0} = (\pi_c + \pi_a) - (\pi_a) = \pi_c
\]
The denominator is simply the proportion of compliers in the population.


Step 4: Combining the Numerator and Denominator
Now we assemble the final IV estimand ratio:
\[
\text{IV Estimand} = \frac{\E{Y|Z=1} - \E{Y|Z=0}}{\E{A|Z=1} - \E{A|Z=0}} = \frac{(\E{Y(1)|c} - \E{Y(0)|c}) \cdot \pi_c}{\pi_c}
\]
The \(\pi_c\) terms cancel, leaving our final result:
\[
\text{IV Estimand} = \E{Y(1)|c} - \E{Y(0)|c}
\]
This proves that under the IV assumptions, the formula precisely calculates the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE): the average causal effect of the treatment only for the subpopulation of compliers.
The relationship between what we can see (observed outcomes) and what could have happened (potential outcomes) is the foundation of modern causal inference. It allows us to use real-world data to answer “what if” questions.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV) Estimation
text:
The Core Assumption: Consistency
The primary rule connecting observed and potential outcomes is the consistency assumption. It states that an individual’s observed outcome is simply their potential outcome corresponding to the treatment they actually received.

For the Outcome (Y): If an individual receives treatment \(A=a\), their observed outcome \(Y\) is equal to their potential outcome \(Y(a)\).

If you take the medicine (\(A=1\)), the headache level you experience (\(Y\)) is precisely your potential headache level had you taken the medicine (\(Y(1)\)).
If you don’t take the medicine (\(A=0\)), the headache level you experience (\(Y\)) is your potential headache level had you not taken it (\(Y(0)\)).

For the Treatment (A): The same logic applies if there’s an instrument (\(Z\)) influencing the treatment. If an individual is exposed to instrument level \(Z=z\), their observed treatment status \(A\) is equal to their potential treatment status \(A(z)\).

If you are encouraged by your doctor to get a vaccine (\(Z=1\)), your observed vaccination status (\(A\)) is your potential status had you been encouraged (\(A(1)\)).


Without this assumption, we couldn’t link the data we collect to the causal effects we want to estimate. Consistency is one half of the broader Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA), with the other half being “no interference” between individuals.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV) Estimation
text:
Mathematical Formulation
We can express these relationships with simple formulas. For a binary treatment (\(A \in \{0, 1\}\)):

Outcome Y
The observed outcome \(Y\) is a “switched” version of the two potential outcomes, where the switch is controlled by the observed treatment \(A\):
\[
Y = A \cdot Y(1) + (1-A) \cdot Y(0)
\]
How it works:

If an individual gets the treatment, \(A=1\). The formula becomes \(Y = (1) \cdot Y(1) + (1-1) \cdot Y(0) = Y(1)\).
If an individual does not get the treatment, \(A=0\). The formula becomes \(Y = (0) \cdot Y(1) + (1-0) \cdot Y(0) = Y(0)\).



Treatment A (with an Instrument Z)
Similarly, the observed treatment \(A\) is a switched version of the potential treatment statuses, controlled by the observed instrument \(Z\):
\[
A = Z \cdot A(1) + (1-Z) \cdot A(0)
\]
How it works:

If an individual is exposed to the instrument, \(Z=1\). The formula becomes \(A = (1) \cdot A(1) + (1-1) \cdot A(0) = A(1)\).
If an individual is not exposed to the instrument, \(Z=0\). The formula becomes \(A = (0) \cdot A(1) + (1-0) \cdot A(0) = A(0)\).

These equations are the fundamental link that allows us to take observable quantities (\(Y\), \(A\), \(Z\)) and, under further assumptions like ignorability, make statements about the unobservable causal effects derived from potential outcomes (\(Y(1) - Y(0)\)).

title: Instrumental Variables (IV) Estimation
section: Explaining Expected Value of Observed Y given Observed Instrument
text:
Explaining Expected Value of Observed Y given Observed Instrument
This equality is established by applying the consistency assumption twice, which is the fundamental rule linking observed data to the potential outcomes framework.
Here is a detailed step-by-step explanation.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV) Estimation
text:
Step 1: The Starting Point
We begin with the left side of the equation:
\[
\E{Y|Z=1}
\]
This expression represents the expected (or average) observed outcome \(Y\) among the subgroup of individuals who received the instrument at level 1 (\(Z=1\)).

title: Instrumental Variables (IV) Estimation
section: Step 2: Applying Consistency to the Outcome (Y)
text:
Step 2: Applying Consistency to the Outcome (Y)
The first rule we use is the consistency assumption for the outcome. This rule states that an individual’s observed outcome (\(Y\)) is their potential outcome corresponding to the treatment level (\(A\)) they actually received.

Rule: \(Y = Y(A)\)
Application: We can substitute \(Y(A)\) for \(Y\) inside our expectation, as they are defined to be equivalent.

\[
\E{Y|Z=1} = \E{Y(A)|Z=1}
\]
This expression now reads: “The expected potential outcome, evaluated at the observed treatment \(A\), for the group where \(Z=1\).”

title: Instrumental Variables (IV) Estimation
section: Step 3: Applying Consistency to the Treatment (A)
text:
Step 3: Applying Consistency to the Treatment (A)
Next, we focus on the observed treatment, \(A\), specifically for the group conditioned on \(Z=1\). The consistency assumption for the treatment states that an individual’s observed treatment status (\(A\)) is their potential treatment status corresponding to the instrument level (\(Z\)) they were actually exposed to.

Rule: \(A = A(Z)\)
Application: For the specific subgroup where \(Z=1\), this rule simplifies to: \(A = A(1)\). This means that for everyone in this group, their observed treatment is equal to their potential treatment had they received the instrument.

title: Instrumental Variables (IV) Estimation
text:
Step 4: Final Substitution
Now we can substitute the result from Step 3 into the expression from Step 2. Since we are working entirely within the subgroup where \(A\) is equivalent to \(A(1)\), we can replace \(A\) with \(A(1)\) inside the potential outcome function.
\[
\E{Y(A)|Z=1} = \E{Y(A(1))|Z=1}
\]
By chaining these steps together, we show the full equality:
\[
\E{Y|Z=1} \xrightarrow{\text{Consistency on Y}} \E{Y(A)|Z=1} \xrightarrow{\text{within the Z=1 group}}_{\text{Consistency on A }} \E{Y(A(1))|Z=1}
\]
This final expression, \(\E{Y(A(1))|Z=1}\), represents the expected potential outcome that results from the potential treatment an individual would choose if exposed to the instrument.

title: Week 6: Propensity Score Methods (Revised)
text:
In a perfect world, we would answer all causal questions using a Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT). By randomly assigning treatment, we ensure that, on average, the treated and control groups are identical on all background characteristics (both observed and unobserved). Any difference in their outcomes can therefore be attributed to the treatment.
However, in public health and clinical research, RCTs are often unethical, impractical, or too expensive. We must rely on observational data, where individuals select their own treatments. This leads to a critical problem: people who choose treatment are often systematically different from those who do not.
This week, we introduce propensity score methods, a powerful toolkit designed to address this selection bias. Propensity scores allow us to mimic the properties of an RCT by creating balanced comparison groups, helping us to isolate the causal effect of a treatment from the confounding effects of other variables.
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Define the propensity score and explain its central role in causal inference.
Understand and explain the balancing property of the propensity score and why it is crucial for creating comparable groups.
Estimate propensity scores using logistic regression and other methods.
Implement three core propensity score methods: matching, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and stratification.
Assess whether a propensity score model has successfully balanced the covariates between the treated and control groups using diagnostic plots and tables.
Critically evaluate the advantages and limitations of propensity score methods and their underlying assumptions.






Imagine we want to know the effect of a new fitness program (treatment D=1) on weight loss (outcome Y). In our observational data, people who joined the program lost more weight. But can we conclude the program caused the weight loss?
Probably not. The people who chose to join are likely different. They might be younger, more health-conscious, or have better access to healthy food. This is confounding. We are comparing a group of motivated “apples” to a general population of “oranges.”
The goal of propensity scores is to solve this problem by creating a “handicap” system. Instead of trying to match people on dozens of characteristics (age, gender, income, diet, etc.), we can boil all of that information down into a single number: the propensity score.




The propensity score is the probability that a unit (e.g., a person) receives the treatment, given their observed baseline covariates.

\[
e(X_i) = P(D_i = 1 | X_i)
\]
Where:

\(D\_i = 1\) if person i receives the treatment.
\(X\_i\) is the vector of all observed pre-treatment covariates for person i (e.g., age, gender, baseline health status).

Think of it like this: if someone has a propensity score of 0.8, it means that based on their observed characteristics, they had an 80% chance of being in the treatment group. A person with a score of 0.1 had only a 10% chance.



This is the theoretical cornerstone that makes propensity scores so powerful.

Theorem (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983): If we correctly specify the propensity score model, then within strata of the propensity score, the distribution of the observed covariates X is independent of treatment status D.

\[
(Y^1, Y^0) \perp D | X \implies (Y^1, Y^0) \perp D | e(X)
\]
In plain language: If you take a treated person and an untreated person who have the exact same propensity score, you can think of them as being “statistically equivalent” on all the observed covariates that went into the score. It’s as if, for that pair of individuals, the treatment was randomly assigned. By conditioning on this single score, we have “balanced” all the observed confounders simultaneously.






Key Assumption: Ignorability & Positivity




Ignorability (or Unconfoundedness): We must assume that we have measured and included all common causes of the treatment and the outcome in our propensity score model. Propensity scores cannot balance unobserved confounders (e.g., genetic factors, motivation).
Positivity (or Overlap): For any set of covariates X, there must be a non-zero probability of being both treated and untreated. \(0 < P(D=1 | X=x) < 1\). If a certain type of person always gets the treatment, we have no one to compare them to.







Let’s make this extremely simple. Imagine we have 6 patients. We want to know if a new drug (D=1) helps reduce blood pressure (Y). We know that age (X) is a confounder: older people have higher blood pressure and are also more likely to get the new drug.
